title: API Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of api design and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—public versus internal apis—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study api design with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you keep a Java codebase understandable as its responsibilities and collaborators grow. In this lesson, focus on public versus internal apis and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect public versus internal apis with consistent naming before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Public versus internal APIs
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

items.title: Consistent naming
items.text: Maintainable design makes responsibilities, contracts, and dependency direction clear. Prefer cohesive components and focused interfaces, applying patterns and SOLID principles when they solve a real problem. Apply that reasoning specifically to consistent naming and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Preconditions and postconditions
items.text: Control flow decides which statements run and how often. Make conditions precise, set clear loop termination conditions, and test zero/one/many-item boundaries to catch off-by-one errors.

items.title: Error contracts
items.text: Maintainable design makes responsibilities, contracts, and dependency direction clear. Prefer cohesive components and focused interfaces, applying patterns and SOLID principles when they solve a real problem. Apply that reasoning specifically to error contracts and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Compatibility and evolution
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Separate domain decisions from input/output so logic can be tested directly. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: apply api design to a small project artifact. Record the trade-off, one verification step, and a rollback or recovery path where relevant.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one listed topic from API Design.
The learner states the expected result before running or inspecting the example.
At least one boundary, failure, compatibility, or maintainability consideration is documented where relevant.
hints: Start by identifying the contract or rule behind public versus internal apis.
Reduce the example to the smallest input that makes the behavior visible.
Test one boundary or failure case and compare the result with the expected behavior.
content.execution_notes: Java requires a JDK or a separate isolated server runner. No Java sandbox is bundled with this content; never execute learner code inside the FastAPI process or public production container.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.

summary: API Design is best understood by connecting its contract to a small observable example.
Key syllabus points: Public versus internal APIs, Consistent naming, Preconditions and postconditions.
Use official versioned documentation and tests to confirm assumptions before relying on behavior in a larger application.
